description_full: Parsons Corporation provides design, engineering and technical services, and smart and agile software for the United States federal government and critical infrastructure customers worldwide. It operates through Federal Solutions and Critical Infrastructure segments. The Federal Solutions segment offers critical technologies, such as cyber; air and missile defense; intelligence; aviation modernization; electronic warfare; space ground systems, cislunar, A-PNT, and classified sensors; geospatial and signals intelligence; environmental remediation; border security and counter-drug, critical infrastructure protection; counter unmanned air systems; biometrics; and bio surveillance solutions. This segment also provides software and hardware, and technical expertise; satellite ground systems support and operations, flight dynamics, data fusion and analytics, platform system integration, directed energy, joint all-domain operations, and command and control systems; digital landscape, including full-spectrum cyber, defensive cyber operations, information operations, and analytics; and electronic warfare, multi-domain operations, mission support and national to tactical operations, as well as cyber solutions and products. The Critical Infrastructure segment develops digital solutions for aviation, rail and transit, bridges, roads, highways, and urban destinations. This segment also provides planning, engineering, and management services for complex infrastructure comprising bridges, tunnels, roads and highways, and water and wastewater systems; intelligent transportation systems, utilities, environmental remediation, emerging contaminants, aviation, and rail and transit, as well as ParsonsX, a digital transformation organization; and multi-disciplinary design, technical, and management solutions. Parsons Corporation was founded in 1944 and is headquartered in Chantilly, Virginia.

financial_summary: Parsons Corporation is a mid-cap technology business with a $5.2B market cap on $6.4B of annual revenue.
The top line has compounded at +15% over the past three years, the kind of sustained demand persistence that marks a compounder.
Returns on capital run at 9% against a 8% cost of capital, which means the business barely earns its keep economically.

The business throws off $410M in free cash flow — roughly 6 cents on every revenue dollar, which is the owner-earnings figure that actually belongs to shareholders, and cash conversion sits at 1.98× so those profits are backed by real cash.
On the balance sheet, leverage is comfortably conservative at 1.4× net debt/EBITDA, and interest coverage runs at 8.1×.

Shareholder yield of 2.2% reflects a genuine commitment to returning capital rather than empire-building, and insider ownership is negligible, so management has little personal stake in the long-term outcome, and profit capture is only 0.3× the fair share, suggesting no structural edge inside its industry.

val: The stock trades 57% below its DCF fair value of $114, a meaningful margin of safety.

Against its own history it is cheap: the EBIT multiple sits 45% below its 10-year median.
Earnings yields are mixed: an FCF yield of 7.8% (above the risk-free rate) and an EBIT/EV of 6.3% (vs the 8% bar).
The 11 covering analysts target $61.36 on average, 23% above the price, well away from the model's fair value.
prof: ROIC of 9% earns above the cost of capital of 8.0%, but the 1pp spread is short of the 7pp moat bar; returns have been steady (CV 0.28).
It converts 6% of revenue into free cash flow.

hlth: Leverage is conservative at 1.4x net debt to EBITDA ($466.4M of cash against $1.2B of debt), with interest covered 8.1x.

growth: Revenue has compounded at 14.9% over 3 years and 10.2% over 5 years, so growth is accelerating, and it has been lumpy (year-to-year swings of 14%).
At current returns, reinvesting 100% of profits supports about 8.6% a year of fundamental growth, enough to sustain growth.
Free cash flow has compounded 10.0% a year over five years.
Forward indicators: a book-to-bill of 1.06 (orders outpacing sales), a backlog worth 1.1x annual revenue and deferred revenue up 17%.
Capex runs only 0.6x depreciation (1.1% of sales), so the asset base is being harvested rather than grown.
Its Rule of 40 score is 16, below the 40 that marks a healthy growth business.
own: Insiders own a modest 1.5%, and reported institutional holdings exceed 100% of shares (a sign of heavy share lending).
Insiders have only bought over the past year (7 purchases, net $3.1M bought).
It returns 2.2% a year to shareholders (2.2% in buybacks).
The share count has grown 11.3% a year over five years, diluting existing holders.
Short interest is elevated at 15.2% of the float, 4.4 days to cover.
people: With about 21,000 employees, each generates about $303K of revenue, 0.8x the Technology median, and revenue has grown 8.3% a year across its filed history.

CEO pay is $2.8M (9x revenue per employee), and compensation governance scores well (2/10, lower is better).
